input.title: Hardy, "The Darkling Thrush": A Hope Imagined but Not Shared
input.addressed: leans on a gate at dusk in a frozen winter landscape and unexpectedly hears an old, frail thrush burst into song
input.focus: convey the speaker's guarded shift from a desolation he reads into the land around him toward a hope he can imagine in the bird's song but cannot himself claim
input.rubric: <parameter name="rows">[{"row_id":"A","task_specific":"A defensible thesis must make a claim about how the speaker's attitude moves or stays divided, for example that the thrush's song unsettles the speaker's despair without overturning it, or that the hope he names stays the bird's and never fully becomes his. Saying only that the poem moves from sadness to happiness, or that the poem is about winter and a bird, does not count, because it ignores the qualified ending ('I could think', 'I was unaware'). A thesis that names devices without making a claim about the speaker's attitude does not earn the point. A thesis may argue for real but tentative hope, or for a hope that only makes the speaker's isolation clearer, as long as it is arguable and fits the text."},{"row_id":"B","task_specific":"Strong responses trace the poem's structure: in the first two stanzas the speaker projects death onto the landscape (the spectral Frost, 'The weakening eye of day', the Century's corpse with 'His crypt the cloudy canopy', the 'broken lyres'), and the second stanza closes on 'Seemed fervourless as I'. That line shows the gloom comes partly from the speaker himself. Strong responses then analyze the turn at 'At once a voice outburst' and the contrast between the bird's body ('aged', 'frail, gaunt, and small', 'blast-beruffled') and its song ('full-hearted evensong', 'joy illimited'). They should also look closely at the final stanza's hedged syntax and diction ('could think', 'Some blessed Hope', 'he knew / And I was unaware'). A score of 4 requires commentary that keeps tying these choices to the guarded, divided attitude, for example by showing that the broken lyres of stanza one are answered by a living song that the speaker hears but cannot interpret. A 3 explains relevant evidence with some uneven links to the claim. A 2 mostly summarizes, or lists devices with general comments. A 1 offers little relevant evidence or makes mostly inaccurate claims."},{"row_id":"C","task_specific":"Sophistication here might mean tracking the tension in the ending instead of settling it. A response could show that the speaker's admission 'I was unaware' gives the hope reality while also shutting him out of it. It could note that his projections in stanzas one and two ('seemed to be', 'Seemed') prepare us to doubt his reading of the bird too. Or it could argue that 'darkling' and 'growing gloom' keep the darkness present even as the song rises. A vivid but general style, or passing mentions of historical context, does not earn the point by itself. The insight has to come from close reading and run through the whole argument."}]
scoring_notes: Do not reward readings that claim the speaker is converted to confident faith or joy. The final stanza's 'could think' and 'unaware' must be accounted for, though an essay may argue that some hope is real.

The reading of the Century's corpse as the end of an era is supported by the text and fair to use. Essays should not be rewarded for outside biographical or historical claims they do not tie to the poem's language.
Accurate use of terms is not required. An essay that describes the effect of the contrast between the bird's frailty and its song without naming 'juxtaposition' can still earn full Row B credit.
Essays that treat the stanzas in order can score well if the commentary builds a line of reasoning about the attitude and doesn't just paraphrase.

defensible_positions: The thrush's song interrupts but does not cancel the speaker's despair: the hope he senses stays conditional ('could think') and belongs to the bird, which leaves the speaker more aware of his own isolation.

The speaker's desolation is partly a projection, as 'seemed' and 'fervourless as I' show, so the bird's song shows up the limits of his own perception and makes room for a hope beyond what he can see.

The poem sets lifeless art and life against each other: the 'broken lyres' of the landscape give way to a real 'evensong', which suggests that song and spirit can survive in a dying world even if the speaker cannot join in.

The bird's choice to sing despite age and cold ('Had chosen thus to fling his soul') presents hope as an act of will rather than a reaction to evidence, which the speaker admires but cannot perform himself.
The ending is ambivalent on purpose: by naming 'Some blessed Hope' only to admit he is 'unaware' of it, the speaker keeps both hope and doubt alive without settling the question.

devices.effect: Picturing the landscape as a dead body laid in a tomb of cloud makes the whole scene a funeral and shows how completely the speaker reads death into the world.
Comparing the vines to snapped instrument strings suggests that music, art, and inspiration have failed. This sets up the surprise of the thrush's living song.
The fading sun as a failing eye joins nightfall to failing vision and hints at the speaker's own limited perception.
'Seemed' and the comparison to himself show that the bleakness is partly the speaker's projection, which makes his despair less objective than it first appears.

devices.quote: At once a voice outburst among
devices.effect: The sudden 'outburst' breaks the deathly stillness and turns the poem from description of a dead world to an encounter with life.

devices.quote: An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small
devices.effect: Piling up words of frailty right after 'joy illimited' sets the bird's weak body against its boundless song, so its hope seems to defy circumstance.
Singing becomes a bold, self-giving act thrown against 'the growing gloom', which presents hope as a choice rather than a response to the world.

devices.quote: Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew / And I was unaware.
devices.effect: The closing lines grant that the Hope exists only to place it outside the speaker's knowledge, so the poem ends divided between possibility and exclusion.

common_pitfalls: Summarizing the poem as a simple move from sadness to happiness and ignoring the hedged final stanza.
Spotting devices (personification, alliteration) without explaining how they shape the speaker's attitude.
Making large claims about the author's beliefs or historical events that the poem's language doesn't support.
Treating the first two stanzas as only setting and missing that 'seemed' marks the gloom as the speaker's own reading.
Saying the bird has religious faith as plain fact, when the speaker only 'could think' it holds 'Some blessed Hope'.

blueprint.central_idea: A speaker who sees the dead century and his own lack of spirit everywhere in a winter landscape is interrupted by an old thrush's ecstatic song. He finds himself able to imagine a hope he cannot verify or share.
blueprint.complexity: The poem's turn is real but limited. The song breaks the deathly scene, yet the speaker's 'could think' and 'unaware' keep the hope at a distance. And the early 'seemed' clauses show his despair is partly projection, so both his despair and his hope are open to question.
